claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of uIPSCs from P12-13 to P14-15, as shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Eye opening does not affect the strength of uIPSCs from Sst-INs to interneurons in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
claims.source: Here, we show that coinciding with eye opening, the strength of unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) from somatostatin-expressing interneurons (Sst-INs) to nearby excitatory neurons, but not interneurons, sharply decreases in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Sst-IN→FS-IN and Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs during eye opening, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The strength of uIPSCs from fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) to excitatory neurons significantly increases during eye opening.
claims.source: In contrast, the strength of uIPSCs from fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) to excitatory neurons significantly increases during eye opening.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a ~140% increase in FS-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15, as shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Dark rearing prevents the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission that occur during eye opening.
claims.source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Sst-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude between P12-13 and P14-15 in dark-reared mice, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Binocular lid suture prevents the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission that occur during eye opening.
claims.source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in synaptic transmission in continuously sutured mice, as shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Artificial opening of sutured lids reproduces the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
claims.source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that artificially eye-opened mice exhibit decreased Sst-IN→PC and increased FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission, as shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The differential maturation of synaptic transmission from Sst-INs and FS-INs to PCs is accompanied by a significant change in the postsynaptic quantal size.
claims.source: Mechanistically, this differential maturation of synaptic transmission is accompanied by a significant change in the postsynaptic quantal size.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis showing that postsynaptic quantal size (Q) decreases in Sst-IN→PC connections and increases in FS-IN→PC connections during eye opening, as shown in Figure 7H and 7P.

claims.claim: Sensory experience critically influences neuronal connectivity and synaptic transmission during neocortical development.
claims.source: During neocortical development, sensory experience critically inﬂuences neuronal connectivity and synaptic transmission (Katz and Shatz, 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Katz and Shatz, 1996.

claims.claim: Maturation of the visual cortex depends on visual afferent activity.
claims.source: In the visual system, maturation of the visual cortex depends on visual afferent activity (Hensch, 2005; Hofer et al., 2009; Pecka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensch, 2005; Hofer et al., 2009; Pecka et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Eye opening in rodents typically occurs over a short period of one to two days.
claims.source: Eye opening in rodents typically occurs over a short period of one to two days (Gandhi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gandhi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Eye opening drives a rapid series of changes in neuronal activity, protein trafficking, synaptogenesis, synaptic receptor composition, and synaptic transmission and plasticity.
claims.source: When experimentally synchronized, eye opening drives a rapid series of changes in neuronal activity, protein trafficking, synaptogenesis, synaptic receptor composition, and synaptic transmission and plasticity (Lu and Constantine-Paton, 2004; Yoshii et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu and Constantine-Paton, 2004; Yoshii et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Eye opening affects neuronal circuit development in the retina, superior colliculus, lateral geniculate nucleus, and visual cortex.
claims.source: Moreover, eye opening affects neuronal circuit development in the ascending retinothalamo-cortical pathway at every level: the retina (Feller, 2003; Tian and Copenhagen, 2003), superior colliculus (SC) (Zhao et al., 2006), lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Hooks and Chen, 2006; Levitt et al., 2001), and visual cortex (Hoy and Niell, 2015; Ko et al., 2013; Pecka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining different levels of the visual pathway.

claims.claim: The probability and strength of excitatory connections between layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the visual cortex significantly increased after eye opening.
claims.source: For example, the probability and strength of excitatory connections between layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (PCs) in the visual cortex significantly increased after eye opening, and these changes were prevented by dark rearing (Ishikawa et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishikawa et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Orientation tuning preferences of fast-spiking interneurons were dependent on normal visual experience after eye opening.
claims.source: Although previous study reported that orientation tuning preferences of fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) were dependent on normal visual experience after eye opening (Kuhlman et al., 2011), whether eye opening shapes inhibitory synaptic transmission in the neocortex during development remains unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuhlman et al., 2011.

claims.claim: GABAergic INs in the mature neocortex can be categorized into three main populations based on the expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, and the ionotropic serotonin receptor.
claims.source: In the mature neocortex, GABAergic INs can be categorized into three main populations based on the expression of the calcium-binding protein parvalbumin (PV), the neuropeptide somatostatin (Sst), and the ionotropic serotonin receptor (Lee et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Sst-expressing INs comprise approximately 20-30% of all neocortical INs.
claims.source: Sst-expressing INs (Sst-INs), comprising approximately 20 ~ 30% of all neocortical INs, are among the most prominent GABAergic IN subtypes in the neocortex (Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Sst expression in the superficial neocortex has typically been associated with Martinotti cells.
claims.source: Sst expression in the superficial neocortex has typically been associated with Martinotti cells (MCs)—GABAergic INs with ascending axons that arborize in cortical layer one and spread horizontally to neighboring columns (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Ma et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fino and Yuste, 2011; Ma et al., 2006.

claims.claim: A large fraction of Sst-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PCs.
claims.source: A large fraction of Sst-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Cortical Sst-INs precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs by regulating postsynaptic spine Ca2+ signals, synaptic dynamics, dendritic spike bursts, and transformation of dendritic inputs.
claims.source: In addition to providing lateral inhibition to local PC networks, cortical Sst-INs also precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs by regulating postsynaptic spine Ca2+ signals, synaptic dynamics, dendritic spike bursts, and transformation of dendritic inputs (Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014; Lovett-Barron et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014; Lovett-Barron et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Cortical Sst-INs frequently inhibit other cortical INs (disinhibition).
claims.source: Furthermore, cortical Sst-INs not only innervate PCs but also frequently inhibit other cortical INs (disinhibition) (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claims.claim: PV-expressing FS-INs constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: PV-expressing FS-INs, which constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons, form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claims.claim: PV-expressing FS-INs form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs.
claims.source: PV-expressing FS-INs, which constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons, form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The emergence and maturation of connections from PV-INs to PCs and PV-INs have been reported previously.
claims.source: Although the emergence and maturation of connections from PV-INs to PCs and PV-INs have been reported previously (Lazarus and Huang, 2011); Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011); Yang et al., 2014), the development of inhibitory synaptic transmission (including amplitude and connectivity) from Sst-INs to PCs and other IN subtypes remains largely unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lazarus and Huang, 2011; Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011; Yang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Sst-INs regulate learning-induced and experience-dependent cortical plasticity through feedforward as well as feedback inhibitions, both during early postnatal development and in adulthood.
claims.source: In addition, accumulating evidence indicates that Sst-INs regulate learning-induced and experience-dependent cortical plasticity through feedforward as well as feedback inhibitions, both during early postnatal development and in adulthood (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016.

claims.claim: PV-INs regulate critical-period experience-dependent plasticity.
claims.source: There is also clear evidence suggesting that PV-INs regulate critical-period experience-dependent plasticity (Hensch, 2005; Krishnan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensch, 2005; Krishnan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Approximately 5.2% of tdTomato+ neurons in Sst-tdTomato mice expressed PV.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports (Hu et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013), we observed that ~5.2% of tdTomato+ neurons expressed PV (5.2 ± 0.3%, nine slices from three mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and citations to Hu et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Approximately 17.2% of tdTomato+ neurons showed FS properties.
claims.source: Meanwhile, ~17.2% of tdTomato+ neurons showed the FS properties (36 out of 209, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Hu et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and citations to Hu et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015.

claims.claim: FS tdTomato+ cells exhibited the distinctive basket cell morphology.
claims.source: Furthermore, FS tdTomato+ cells exhibited the distinctive basket cell morphology (4 out of 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Non-FS tdTomato+ cells were characterized by morphological properties including ascending axonal arborizations with extensive branching in layer one and horizontal collaterals, consistent with Martinotti cells.
claims.source: Non-FS tdTomato+ cells were further characterized by morphological properties, including ascending axonal arborizations with extensive branching in layer one and horizontal collaterals (19 out of 20, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), consistent with those of Martinotti cells as previously described (Fino and Yuste, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Fino and Yuste, 2011.

claims.claim: Sst-IN→PC connections emerged at postnatal day 7-8 (P7-8).
claims.source: We found that Sst-IN→PC connections emerged at postnatal day 7–8 (P7–8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings at different developmental stages.

claims.claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses increased significantly from P7-8 to P9-11.
claims.source: The connection probability increased significantly from P7–8 to P9–11 (χ2 test, p=0.0046; Figure 1E) and remained largely comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.149; Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.0046).

claims.claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses remained largely comparable from P9 to P20.
claims.source: The connection probability increased significantly from P7–8 to P9–11 (χ2 test, p=0.0046; Figure 1E) and remained largely comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.149; Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.149).

claims.claim: There was a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs from P12-13 to P14-15.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of uIPSCs from P12–13 to P14–15 (P7–8, 17.9 ± 2.9 pA; P9–11, 28.3 ± 5.4 pA; P12–13, 34.3 ± 4.8 pA; P14–15, 11.6 ± 1.8 pA; P16–17, 10.0 ± 1.4 pA; P18–20, 6.0 ± 1.9 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(5,185) = 8.788, p=1.7 × 10−7; Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(5,185) = 8.788, p=1.7 × 10−7).

claims.claim: The dramatic change in Sst-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude coincided with the natural eye opening of mice under standard living conditions.
claims.source: Notably, this dramatic change coincided with the natural eye opening of mice under standard living conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the weakening of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs may result from eye opening.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the timing of eye opening in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and the timing of uIPSC amplitude changes in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The 10-90% rise time of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P18-20 was significantly longer than that at P7-8 and P12-13.
claims.source: Although the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs at P18–20 was significantly longer than that at P7–8 and P12–13, the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9–17 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The 10-90% rise time of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9-17.
claims.source: Although the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs at P18–20 was significantly longer than that at P7–8 and P12–13, the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9–17 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The half-width of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs did not show any obvious change at P7-20.
claims.source: Furthermore, the half-width of uIPSCs did not show any obvious change at P7–20 (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The total length and complexity of both apical and basal dendrites of PCs exhibited no significant difference between P12-13 and P14-15 mice.
claims.source: In addition, the total length and complexity of both apical and basal dendrites of PCs exhibited no significant difference between P12–13 and P14–15 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–I), suggesting that dendritic morphology of PCs remains unchanged during eye opening.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-I.

claims.claim: The connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission exhibited similar development properties when using cesium-based and high Cl- internal solution to record the postsynaptic currents.
claims.source: Of note, the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission exhibited similar development properties when we used cesium-based and high Cl- internal solution to record the postsynaptic currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 was significantly smaller than that at P12-13 in the prefrontal Cg1/2 area.
claims.source: Consistent with the result observed in the visual cortex, the peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 was significantly smaller than that at P12–13 in Cg1/2 (P9–11, 31.6 ± 6.6 pA; P12–13, 31.0 ± 4.7 pA; P14–15, 11.0 ± 3.1 pA; P16–17, 5.0 ± 1.9 pA; P18–20, 5.7 ± 1.0 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(4,46) = 5.51, p=6.0 × 10−4; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(4,46) = 5.51, p=6.0 × 10−4).

claims.claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses in Cg1/2 remained comparable from P9 to P20.
claims.source: The connection probability remained comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.857; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.857).

claims.claim: The weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission during eye opening exists not only in the visual cortex but also in Cg1/2.
claims.source: These results suggest that the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission during eye opening exists not only in the visual cortex but also in Cg1/2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both visual cortex (Figure 1) and Cg1/2 (Figure 2) showing similar developmental changes.

claims.claim: 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12-18 in Sst-tdTomato::Lhx6-EGFP mice.
claims.source: We found that 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12–18 (87 out of 111, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and these FS-INs showed basket cell morphology (15 out of 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: FS-INs in Sst-tdTomato::Lhx6-EGFP mice showed basket cell morphology.
claims.source: We found that 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12–18 (87 out of 111, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and these FS-INs showed basket cell morphology (15 out of 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses did not significantly change from P12 to P18.
claims.source: The connection probability did not significantly change from P12 to P18 (χ2 test, p=0.949; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.949).

claims.claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 and P16-18 was significantly stronger than that at P12-13.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P16–18 was significantly stronger than that at P12–13 (P12–13, 91 ± 14 pA; P14–15, 217 ± 37 pA; P16–18, 279 ± 57 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(2,63) = 8.71, p=4.6 × 10−4; Figure 3E), suggesting that eye opening may increase the FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(2,63) = 8.71, p=4.6 × 10−4).

claims.claim: The 10-90% rise time and half-width of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12-13 and P14-15.
claims.source: Moreover, the 10–90% rise time and half-width of uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12–13 and P14–15, while the rise time was significantly shorter at P16–18 than at P12–13 (Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: The 10-90% rise time of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs was significantly shorter at P16-18 than at P12-13.
claims.source: Moreover, the 10–90% rise time and half-width of uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12–13 and P14–15, while the rise time was significantly shorter at P16–18 than at P12–13 (Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 and P17-20 was significantly larger than that at P12-13 in Cg1/2 area.
claims.source: In Cg1/2 area, we also observed a significantly larger peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P17–20 than that at P12–13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while the connection probability was comparable among the three groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses in Cg1/2 was comparable among P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 groups.
claims.source: In Cg1/2 area, we also observed a significantly larger peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P17–20 than that at P12–13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while the connection probability was comparable among the three groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The Sst-IN→FS-IN connection probability did not change from P12 to P18.
claims.source: Our data showed that the Sst-IN→FS-IN connection probability did not change from P12 to P18 (χ2 test, p=0.855; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.855).

claims.claim: The strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs did not exhibit any obvious change from P12 to P18.
claims.source: Notably, the strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs did not exhibit any obvious change (P12–13, 62.0 ± 12.7 pA; P14–15, 72.1 ± 18.7 pA; P16–18, 56.6 ± 13.0 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(2,24) = 0.268, p=0.767, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(2,24) = 0.268, p=0.767).

claims.claim: Htr3a-INs are the predominant type of INs in the superficial visual layers, comprising ~50% of layer 2/3 INs.
claims.source: Htr3a-INs are the predominant type of INs in the superficial visual layers, comprising ~50% of layer 2/3 INs (Lee et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claims.claim: 5HT3a receptors in the neocortex are present exclusively in GABAergic INs.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that 5HT3a receptors (encoded by Htr3a) in the neocortex are present exclusively in GABAergic INs (Lee et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Only ~1% of tdTomato+ Sst-INs expressed EGFP in Sst-tdTomato::Htr3a-EGFP mice.
claims.source: Only ~1% of tdTomato+ Sst-INs expressed EGFP (1.1 ± 0.7%, six slices from three mice), suggesting that Sst-INs and Htr3a-INs are two different types of INs as previously reported (Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry and citations to Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9-11.
claims.source: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9–11, and the probability of connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17 (χ2 test, p=0.169; Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The probability of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17.
claims.source: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9–11, and the probability of connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17 (χ2 test, p=0.169; Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.169).

claims.claim: There was no obvious difference in the strength of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs between P12-13 and P14-15 mice.
claims.source: Similar to Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs, there was no obvious difference in the strength of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs between P12–13 (before eye opening) and P14–15 (after eye opening) mice (P9–11, 19.1 ± 6.8 pA; P12–13, 21.9 ± 7.4 pA; P14–15, 25.6 ± 8.5 pA; P16–17, 28.6 ± 9.9 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(3,37) = 0.183, p=0.907; Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,37) = 0.183, p=0.907).

claims.claim: The connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs exhibited no significant difference among P12-13, P14-15, and P16-19 groups.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that the connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs exhibited no significant difference among P12–13, P14–15, and P16–19 groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs and FS-INs exhibited no significant difference at P12-13.
claims.source: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs and FS-INs exhibited no significant difference at P12–13 (paired t-test, p=0.510; Figure 5BC and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5B, C, and E with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.510).

claims.claim: At P14-15, the same Sst-INs produced much larger uIPSCs in FS-INs than in PCs.
claims.source: However, at P14–15, the same Sst-INs produced much larger uIPSCs in FS-INs than in PCs (paired t-test, p=0.037; Figures 5B, D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5B, D, and E with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.037).

claims.claim: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs versus that onto Htr3a-INs was not significantly different at P12-13.
claims.source: Similarly, Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs versus that onto Htr3a-INs was not significantly different at P12–13 (paired t-test, p=0.601; Figure 5G and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5G and I with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.601).

claims.claim: Sst-INs produced significantly larger uIPSCs in layer 2/3 Htr3a-INs than in PCs at P14-15.
claims.source: However, Sst-INs produced significantly larger uIPSCs in layer 2/3 Htr3a-INs than in PCs at P14–15 (paired t-test, p=0.037; Figure 5H and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5H and I with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.037).

claims.claim: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses between P12-13 and P14-15.
claims.source: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in connection probability (χ2 test, p=0.066; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) nor unitary strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12–13 and P14–15 (P12–13, 19.6 ± 4.1 pA, n = 13; P14–15, 21.7 ± 3.6 pA, n = 16; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.702; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-reared mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.066).

claims.claim: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in unitary strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12-13 and P14-15.

results.result: Sst-IN→PC connections emerge at P7-8, with connection probability increasing significantly from P7-8 to P9-11 and remaining stable from P9 to P20. Coinciding with eye opening, there is a ~65% reduction in uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 provide comprehensive developmental data showing emergence, maturation, and weakening of Sst-IN→PC connections. The temporal correlation with eye opening (C34) is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing eye opening timing. Statistical analyses (χ² test, one-way ANOVA) support the quantitative claims.

results.result: The weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission during eye opening occurs not only in visual cortex but also in the prefrontal Cg1/2 area, with similar ~65% reduction in uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 demonstrate that the eye opening-dependent weakening of Sst-IN→PC transmission is not restricted to visual cortex. Statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, p=6.0×10⁻⁴) supports the amplitude reduction. This extends the main finding beyond sensory cortex.

results.result: FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission increases during eye opening, with ~140% increase in uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15, while connection probability remains stable. The 10-90% rise time becomes significantly shorter at P16-18.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 provide comprehensive characterization of FS-IN→PC development. The increase in synaptic strength (one-way ANOVA, p=4.6×10⁻⁴) contrasts with Sst-IN→PC weakening. Proper identification of FS-INs (78.4% of EGFP+/tdTomato- cells) and morphological confirmation strengthen the findings.

results.result: FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission also increases during eye opening in the Cg1/2 area, with significantly larger uIPSC amplitude at P14-15 and P17-20 compared to P12-13.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 extend the FS-IN→PC findings to prefrontal cortex, demonstrating that the strengthening is not restricted to visual cortex. This parallels the Sst-IN→PC findings in Cg1/2.

results.result: Synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to other interneurons (FS-INs and Htr3a-INs) does not change during eye opening, with stable connection probability and uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C56-C58 demonstrate cell-type specificity of the eye opening effect. Statistical analyses (one-way ANOVA, p=0.767 for Sst-IN→FS-IN; p=0.907 for Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN) support the lack of change. This specificity is crucial for understanding the circuit reorganization.

results.result: Triple recordings demonstrate that at P12-13, Sst-INs produce similar uIPSCs in PCs and interneurons, but at P14-15, the same Sst-INs produce significantly larger uIPSCs in FS-INs and Htr3a-INs than in PCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 provide direct evidence for target-specific changes using simultaneous recordings from the same presynaptic neuron. Paired t-tests (p=0.037 for both comparisons at P14-15) support the differential inhibition. This is strong evidence for postsynaptic mechanisms.

results.result: Dark rearing from P3 prevents the developmental weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, with no significant changes in connection probability or uIPSC amplitude between P12-13 and P14-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 demonstrate that visual experience is necessary for the weakening. Statistical analyses (χ² test, p=0.066; unpaired t-test, p=0.702) support the lack of change. However, dark rearing eliminates both eye opening and pre-eye opening visual stimulation through closed eyelids.

results.result: Binocular lid suture from P8 prevents the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission in both visual cortex and Cg1/2, while artificial eye opening at P16 reproduces the weakening.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 provide strong evidence that eye opening per se drives the changes. The artificial eye opening experiment (one-way ANOVA, p=0.008 for VC; p=0.003 for Cg1/2) is particularly compelling, demonstrating that the timing can be experimentally controlled.

results.result: Binocular lid suture prevents the strengthening of FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission, while artificial eye opening at P16 reproduces the strengthening in both visual cortex and Cg1/2.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 demonstrate that eye opening also drives FS-IN→PC strengthening. Statistical analyses (one-way ANOVA, p=2.9×10⁻⁴ for VC) support the effect. This complements the Sst-IN→PC findings and demonstrates bidirectional regulation.

results.result: The weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission is mediated by postsynaptic mechanisms, with significant decrease in quantal size (Q) from P12-13 to P14-15 but no changes in presynaptic release probability (PPR, C.V., failure rate) or number of release sites (N).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 provide mechanistic insight through variance-mean analysis. The significant decrease in Q (Mann Whitney U test, p=2.9×10⁻⁴) with stable N (p=0.419) strongly supports postsynaptic mechanisms. The lack of changes in PPR, C.V., and failure rate rules out presynaptic contributions.

results.result: The strengthening of FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission is also mediated by postsynaptic mechanisms, with significant increase in quantal size (Q) from P12-13 to P14-15 but no changes in presynaptic parameters or number of release sites (N).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 demonstrate that FS-IN→PC strengthening also involves postsynaptic mechanisms. The significant increase in Q (unpaired t-test, p=0.026) with stable N (p=0.439) parallels the Sst-IN→PC findings but in the opposite direction.

results.result: In Sst-tdTomato mice, ~5.2% of tdTomato+ neurons express PV and ~17.2% show FS properties with basket cell morphology, while non-FS tdTomato+ cells (95%) exhibit Martinotti cell morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 provide important characterization of the Sst-tdTomato line. The data show heterogeneity in the labeled population, with proper identification and exclusion of FS cells from Sst-IN analysis. This validates the experimental approach.

results.result: The kinetics of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs show minimal changes during eye opening, with 10-90% rise time stable at P9-17 and half-width unchanged at P7-20. PC dendritic morphology also remains unchanged between P12-13 and P14-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 demonstrate that the amplitude changes are not due to alterations in kinetics or dendritic filtering. The stable morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) rules out space-clamp artifacts as an explanation for the amplitude reduction.

results.result: The developmental properties of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission are similar when using cesium-based high Cl- internal solution versus standard potassium-based solution.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 validates the recording conditions. The consistency across different internal solutions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) strengthens confidence in the main findings and addresses potential concerns about driving force and space clamp.

results.result: Only ~1% of tdTomato+ Sst-INs express EGFP in Sst-tdTomato::Htr3a-EGFP mice, confirming that Sst-INs and Htr3a-INs are distinct populations.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 validates the genetic strategy for distinguishing interneuron subtypes. The minimal overlap confirms proper targeting and supports the interpretation of differential effects on different IN populations.

results.result: Eye opening occurs between P13 and P15, with 0% at P13, 77.9±7.4% at P14, and 100% at P15.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 provide essential developmental timeline data. The precise timing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) establishes the temporal correlation between eye opening and synaptic changes, though the 1-2 day window limits precise temporal resolution.

results.result: Eye opening differentially regulates inhibitory synaptic transmission in layer 2/3: weakening Sst-IN→PC transmission, strengthening FS-IN→PC transmission, leaving Sst-IN→interneuron transmission unchanged, with changes mediated by postsynaptic quantal size.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 summarize the main findings. These summary claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including developmental profiling, sensory manipulation, and mechanistic analysis.

results.result: Artificial eye opening can induce the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, and this change is unlikely due to an intrinsic developmental program.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 represent key interpretations supported by the lid suture experiments. The ability to prevent changes by suture and reproduce them by artificial opening strongly argues against an intrinsic developmental program, though complete exclusion of developmental factors is difficult.

results.result: Both connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN and FS-IN→FS-IN synaptic transmission are comparable at P12-13 and P14-15 in continuously sutured mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C83 provide important controls showing that lid suture itself does not alter interneuron-to-interneuron connections. This specificity strengthens the interpretation that eye opening specifically affects interneuron-to-PC connections.

results.result: The average connection probability of Sst-IN→PC connections is ~58% within 100 µm at P12-20, consistent with previous reports in somatosensory cortex (~63%).
results.evaluation: Claim C99 validates the experimental approach by comparison with prior literature. The consistency with Xu et al., 2013 supports the reliability of the measurements, though discrepancies with other studies are noted in the discussion.

results.result: Prior work has established that sensory experience influences cortical development, eye opening drives rapid changes in the visual system, and excitatory connections strengthen after eye opening.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 accurately summarize relevant prior work through appropriate citations. These establish the context for the current study, though the authors should be cautious about over-generalizing from cited work.

results.result: Prior work has characterized the properties and functions of Sst-INs and PV-INs in the neocortex, including their proportions, morphology, connectivity patterns, and roles in plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C25 provide appropriate background on interneuron subtypes through citations. These establish the functional significance of the cell types studied and justify the focus on Sst-INs and FS-INs.

results.result: Htr3a-INs comprise ~50% of layer 2/3 INs, 5HT3a receptors are present exclusively in GABAergic INs, and Htr3a-INs encompass a heterogeneous population including Vip-INs and Npy-INs.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 and C111 accurately cite prior characterization of Htr3a-INs. The acknowledgment of heterogeneity (C111) is important for interpreting the Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN results, as different subtypes may respond differently.

results.result: Prior work shows that GABAergic plasticity during the critical period has been studied, but changes during eye opening are less understood. Previous studies show layer- and region-specific differences in inhibitory development.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C110 appropriately contextualize the current work within prior literature. The discussion of discrepancies between studies (layer differences, regional differences) is important for interpreting the current findings and highlights the novelty of the work.

results.result: GABAA receptors mediate inhibitory transmission, different subunits are selectively inserted at specific synapses, and subunit expression changes during development, potentially explaining the differential changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 accurately cite established knowledge about GABAA receptors. However, C115 is speculative, proposing a mechanism without direct experimental evidence. While plausible, this hypothesis requires testing through receptor subunit analysis or pharmacological experiments.

results.result: The authors propose that decreased Sst-IN→PC inhibition after eye opening enhances visual input by facilitating dendritic events, while increased FS-IN→PC inhibition provides homeostatic rebalancing, potentially important for visual integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 present a functional model based on the data and prior work. While the model is logical and consistent with known functions of these interneuron types, it remains speculative. Claims C118, C120, C122, and C123 are explicitly speculative and require in vivo functional validation.
